newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SOUTH AFRICA'S INFORMAL TRADERS MEAN BUSINESS.
newsitem.headline: SOUTH AFRICA'S INFORMAL TRADERS MEAN BUSINESS.

text.p: As South Africa's high rate of joblessness continues to hurt, informal trading or hawking has become an inevitable way of life for people unable to access the formal job market, a report said on Friday.

The survey conducted in the past six months by Market Research Africa (MRA) said 54 percent of individuals from a sample of 2,507 people -- representing nearly 13.7 million of the country's urban adults -- bought from informal traders more than once a month.

"Although only five in 10 urban South Africans buy goods from street hawkers, eight in 10 feel there is a place for them on the streets of the towns and cities," Hanna Fourie, managing director of MRA, an independent research firm, said a statement.

She said the survey found that buyers were predominantly those in the lower income groups -- earning between 500 and 1,999 rand per month, although there was also a significant percentage of middle class buyers.

"Price may be the main reason people use hawkers," Hanna said adding nearly half -- about 47 percent -- of the people with a monthly household income of 2,000 to 5,999 rand also regularly bought from the hawkers.

Since the demise of apartheid three years ago, South Africa continues to be faced with a battle of huge unemployment, spurred in part by four decades of disparities in skills training and racially mismatched distribution of educational facilites.

President Nelson Mandela's government promises in its Growth, Employment and Redistribution strategy revealed last June to create 400,000 new jobs a year by year 2000, but economists caution that odds seem stacked against its wishes.
Hanna said while many respondents expressed support for the hawkers, they also felt there should be controls.
There are an estimated 25,000 street traders in greater Johannesburg alone.

"There was absolutely no support whatsoever for a suggestion that hawkers be removed from the streets entirely or coralled into specific market areas, (but) eight in 10 people were against hawkers being allowed to set up shops where they pleased," she added.

Established retailers have often complained to local authorities about the impact of uncontrolled informal trading, with hawkers lining pavements and sometimes selling in front of shops selling the same kind of wares.
Hanna said the survey reinforced the need to harmonise relationships between the two sides in view of the important role informal trading appears to be playing in job creation.

"Central business district management and development committees would do well to help hawkers ply their trade in an acceptable way rather than hinder them, or simply hope the problems will go away," she said.
